# MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing

Siyi Qian Affiliation: Peking University Affiliation: Alibaba Token Hub,
Alibaba Group Equal contribution    Hanqing Yang Affiliation: Alibaba
Token Hub, Alibaba Group Equal contribution Corresponding author Project
lead    Weihuang Lin Affiliation: Alibaba Token Hub, Alibaba Group   
Zihao Yang Affiliation: Alibaba Token Hub, Alibaba Group
Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China    Yichen Lu
Affiliation: Zhejiang University    Yuanhong Zheng Affiliation: Peking
University     
Sheng Li Affiliation: Peking University Project lead

###### Abstract

Video editing models achieve strong performance in modifying appearance,
backgrounds, styles, and motions, empowered by large-scale training
data. Beyond general scenarios, professional motions are significant in
performance, sports, and martial arts. This paper focuses on
professional motion editing, which involves fine-grained motion
technique and temporal structure. Given professional motion names but
lacking detailed descriptions, existing models often fail to generate
professional motions, such as incorrectly lifting the front wheel under
a Stoppie instruction. To address this challenge, we introduce
MotionCoach, a trained multimodal agent that uses multi-turn tools and
performs self-verification, producing a grounded prompt and a reference
clip as reliable and sufficient multimodal guidance to inject external
professional motion knowledge into video editing models. To supply
training data, we build a data pipeline to construct trajectories. We
cold-start the agent on MotionCoach-SFT-10k and apply Group Relative
Policy Optimization (GRPO) on MotionCoach-RL-2k with rewards on the
motion guidance prompt, the motion outcome video, and the format. For
evaluation, we introduce VPMEBench, comprising 314 professional motion
editing tasks with fine-grained references and annotations. Extensive
experiments show that MotionCoach improves the overall score from 55.1
to 65.6 on Seedance 2.0 and from 51.2 to 64.5 on MiniMax-H3. Learning to
construct multimodal guidance enables precise professional motion
editing without retraining video editing models.

## 1 Introduction

Existing video editing methods make advances on object replacement,
background modification, and style transfer, benefiting from large-scale
training data \[[Cheng et al., 2024](#bib.bib18), [Jiang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib7), [Bai et al., 2026](#bib.bib8), [Lin et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib10), [Team, 2025](#bib.bib11), [Alibaba Cloud,
2026](#bib.bib13), [Team Seedance et al., 2026](#bib.bib9), [MiniMax,
2026](#bib.bib12)\]. Beyond general scenarios, we study video
professional motion editing, where edited videos must show technically
demanding and complex motions while preserving other source content.
Professional motions are typically composed of named atomic motions that
can be independently identified, such as Twirl & Roll in locking and
White Crane Spreads Its Wings in tai chi. However, existing video
editing models often generate an incorrect motion. For example, a
Stoppie request instead produces a Wheelie, reversing the required
support relationship
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")).
Correct motions require appropriate technique and temporal structure,
including body coordination, support, and stage order or a key pose. A
short instruction rarely specifies these details, while the editing
models lack the knowledge coverage required for professional motions in
vertical scenarios.

Addressing this gap requires supplying external guidance that specifies
the professional motion technique. Constructing reliable and sufficient
guidance is challenging, which requires presenting the target motion
correctly, clearly, and completely. Some video editing models supplement
text instructions with references for concrete visual details \[[Jiang
et al., 2025](#bib.bib7), [Lin et al., 2026a](#bib.bib10)\], but
standard task formulations assume that suitable reference is already
available, leaving guidance acquisition and verification outside the
task. Some visual-generation methods use search to acquire external
information \[[Bian et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)\], but relevance alone
does not guarantee reliable guidance. Together, these limitations leave
the problem of constructing reliable and sufficient guidance unresolved.

![Refer to caption](2610.12963v1/motivation.png)

Figure 1: Motivation for professional motion editing. Prompting Seedance
2.0 \[[Team Seedance et al., 2026](#bib.bib9)\] with _Change the rider’s
motion to Stoppie_ yields a Wheelie (wrong wheel lifted). MotionCoach
instead supplies a grounded prompt and reference clip specifying the
correct technique.

To address this problem, we introduce MotionCoach, a trained autonomous
multimodal agent that learns to perform multi-turn tool use and verify
references to obtain reliable and sufficient guidance for professional
motion editing. The agent searches for professional demonstrations,
inspects candidates for the target technique, and clips a clear
target-motion interval. Self-verification then assesses motion
correctness, visibility, and completeness from the clip, triggering
reselection or temporal adjustment. The agent constructs a grounded
prompt from the verified demonstration and source video. Together, the
verified clip and grounded prompt form generator-friendly guidance that
conveys the motion technique and temporal structure to the video editing
model.

Given the scarcity of multi-turn agent trajectories for professional
motion guidance, we build a data pipeline where a teacher model
generates trajectories with tools and self-verification, filtered by
vision-language model (VLM) checks and human spot-checking, yielding
MotionCoach-SFT-10k and MotionCoach-RL-2k. Based on these, we train the
agent in two stages. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) equips the agent with
basic formatting and tool-use capabilities, which are subsequently
refined through agentic reinforcement learning (RL) via Group Relative
Policy Optimization (GRPO) \[[Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib16)\].
Specifically, RL leverages three rewards for the motion guidance prompt,
the motion outcome video, and the format, with the video reward scoring
what the frozen editing model produces in each rollout. The feedback
updates only the agent, improving its selection and organization of
reliable and sufficient motion knowledge.

Additionally, to evaluate professional motion correctness in edited
videos, we introduce VPMEBench, 314 human-verified editing tasks across
25 professional motion categories in dance, sports, and martial arts. We
construct the benchmark using professional demonstrations, VLM
verification, and human annotations. Each task provides evaluation
references, namely a verified reference clip, selected semantic
keyframes, and annotations of temporal structure, motion technique, and
negative constraints. Evaluation uses a VLM as the judge, scoring motion
professionalism (MP), physical plausibility (PP), and overall video
quality (VQ) against these references.

Experiments show that MotionCoach improves professional motion editing.
On VPMEBench, overall scores increase from 55.1 to 65.6 for Seedance 2.0
and from 51.2 to 64.5 for MiniMax-H3 on a 100-point scale. Ablations
support the contribution of agent training and the benefits of combining
grounded prompt with reference clip for motion professionalism.
Constructing multimodal guidance with an agent therefore secures
guidance reliability and sufficiency, raising the professional
correctness of edited motions.

The main contributions are summarized as follows.

- •
  MotionCoach, an agentic framework that performs multi-turn tool use
  and self-verification to construct reliable and sufficient multimodal
  guidance for video editing models.
- •
  MotionCoach-SFT-10k, MotionCoach-RL-2k, and VPMEBench. We construct
  datasets for training alongside a human-verified benchmark for
  professional motion evaluation.
- •
  Overall performance gains across MiniMax-H3 and Seedance 2.0 on
  VPMEBench, empowering video editing models to enhance professional
  motion editing performance.

## 2 Related Work

![Refer to caption](2610.12963v1/data_pipeline.png)

Figure 2: Illustration of the data pipeline. (1) Data preparation
prepares source videos and edit prompts. (2) Agentic trajectory
construction acquires and verifies motion references to produce
MotionCoach-SFT-10k and MotionCoach-RL-2k. (3) Human-verified benchmark
construction establishes VPMEBench.

Video editing. Video editing models support increasingly diverse
changes. Among open-source approaches, InsV2V and Ditto learn
instruction-guided editing from synthetic paired data \[[Cheng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib18), [Bai et al., 2026](#bib.bib8)\], Lucy-Edit-Dev
targets clothing, character, and scene changes \[[Team,
2025](#bib.bib11)\], and VACE and Kiwi-Edit support
reference-conditioned editing \[[Jiang et al., 2025](#bib.bib7), [Lin et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib10)\]. Richer multimodal inputs also support
general-purpose generation and editing in MiniMax-H3 and the
closed-source Seedance 2.0 and HappyHorse 1.0 \[[MiniMax,
2026](#bib.bib12), [Team Seedance et al., 2026](#bib.bib9), [Alibaba
Cloud, 2026](#bib.bib13)\]. However, professional motion editing remains
challenging for these models, which often fail to generate technically
demanding motions.

Agentic visual generation and editing. One line of agentic methods
orchestrates pretrained models at inference time, using planning,
feedback, and external knowledge to organize visual generation and
editing \[[Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib19), [Ye et al.,
2026](#bib.bib20), [Yao et al., 2026](#bib.bib21), [He et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22), [Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)\]. Among these, RS-Gen
retrieves external knowledge for image generation, and VideoAgent
combines shot planning, asset search, and temporal trimming for video
editing \[[Bian et al., 2026](#bib.bib15), [Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib27)\]. Another line trains agent policies to connect
decisions with visual outcomes \[[Jiang et al., 2026](#bib.bib23), [Lin
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib24), [Chen et al., 2026a](#bib.bib25), [Zhang et
al., 2026](#bib.bib14)\]. Agentic methods are increasingly used in image
generation, but video generation and editing remain comparatively
underexplored. These results motivate learning to construct editing
conditions, while motion technique and temporal structure stay
unverified.

## 3 Method

### 3.1 Data Construction

![Refer to caption](2610.12963v1/bench.png)

Figure 3: Overview of VPMEBench. 314 professional motion editing tasks
under a hierarchical taxonomy over dance, sports, and martial arts. Each
task provides visual references and textual annotations of the target
motion for evaluation along motion professionalism (MP), physical
plausibility (PP), and overall video quality (VQ).

To provide video editing models with reliable and sufficient multimodal
guidance, a professional motion editing agent must reason over video
observations, execute tools, and verify references, but task-specific
multi-turn data for learning this workflow remain scarce. Therefore, we
design the three-stage pipeline in
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing"),
which prepares source videos and edit prompts, constructs trajectories
that acquire and verify motion guidane, and establishes VPMEBench.

Data preparation and trajectory construction. We collect videos from
online platforms, lasting 5 to 10 seconds at 24 to 60 fps and at 720p or
above. Gemini 3.5 Flash \[[Kavukcuoglu et al., 2026](#bib.bib31)\] then
selects human-centered videos with clear motion and classifies them into
a motion taxonomy of martial arts, sports, and dance. For each
subcategory, GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, and GLM-5.2 \[[OpenAI,
2026](#bib.bib32), [Anthropic, 2026](#bib.bib28), [Z.ai,
2026](#bib.bib29)\] propose professional atomic motions and verify the
names through web search, and each verified motion fills a short
edit-prompt template that defines the editing target of a task. To form
complete professional motion editing tasks, we pair source videos with
edit prompts, assigning two to three source videos per motion to balance
categories. Gemini 3.5 Flash then generates multi-turn ReAct
trajectories \[[Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib17)\] with search, inspect,
and clip tool calls, self-checking the clip to produce the reference
clip and the grounded prompt. We use programmatic checks to validate
tool-call formats and states. A VLM then assesses clip completeness and
grounding faithfulness. Finally, human spot-checks filter the
trajectories. The retained trajectories form MotionCoach-SFT-10k and
MotionCoach-RL-2k. The SFT, RL, and benchmark splits have disjoint
target motion names, source videos, and paired edit prompts.

Benchmark construction. General video editing benchmarks do not provide
comparable references or annotations for named professional atomic
motions
(Table [10](#A1.T10 "Table 10 ‣ A.4 Multi-Turn Agent Loop Example ‣ A.3.4 Motion Outcome Video Reward Judge ‣ A.3.3 Motion Guidance Prompt Reward Prompt ‣ A.3.2 Evaluation Judge Prompt ‣ A.3.1 Agent System Prompt ‣ A.3 Agent Prompts and Tool Schemas ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")
in
Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Benchmark ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")).
To enable fine-grained evaluation of professional motion editing, we
construct VPMEBench with references to motion technique and temporal
structure. Human annotators select demonstrations from professional
tutorials on online platforms for each subcategory. A VLM locates
suitable target-motion intervals, and experts select up to six semantic
keyframes from densely sampled frames per clip. VPMEBench contains 314
professional motion editing tasks across 3 top-level, 10 second-level,
and 25 leaf categories, each taking a source video and an edit prompt as
input and providing fine-grained visual references and textual
annotations of the target motion
(Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 Data Construction ‣ 3 Method ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")
and
Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Benchmark ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")).

We use a VLM as the judge, scoring each dimension 0, 0.5, or 1 from the
generated video, source video, and task references
(Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Benchmark ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")).
Motion professionalism (MP) assesses motion technique and temporal
structure, including stage order or a key pose, while accepting
equivalent executions. Physical plausibility (PP) assesses motion
continuity, balance, limb integrity, and contact consistency. Overall
video quality (VQ) combines video quality and edit preservation at a
ratio of 1:2, covering clarity, temporal stability, and aesthetics as
well as preservation of the subject, scene, and non-target content
beyond the required motion change.

The overall score is

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathrm{Overall}=w_{\mathrm{MP}}\,\mathrm{MP}+w_{\mathrm{PP}}\,\mathrm{PP}+w_{\mathrm{VQ}}\,\mathrm{VQ},
``` |  | (1) |

To emphasize the importance of MP for this task, we set the weights to
$`w_{\mathrm{MP}}=0.5`$, $`w_{\mathrm{PP}}=0.2`$, and
$`w_{\mathrm{VQ}}=0.3`$.

![Refer to caption](2610.12963v1/method.png)

Figure 4: Overview of MotionCoach. Top: the multi-turn agentic loop
during rollout and inference uses search, inspect, and clip tools with
self-verification to produce reliable and sufficient motion guidance.
Bottom: Agentic RL updates the policy with motion guidance prompt,
motion outcome video, and format rewards while keeping the video editing
model frozen.

### 3.2 Agentic Framework

Professional motion editing requires motion technique and temporal
structure. To provide richer external motion knowledge, MotionCoach
takes a source video $`V_{s}`$ and an edit prompt $`u`$, calls the
search, inspect, and clip tools, and verifies the references itself to
produce a grounded prompt $`p`$ and a verified reference clip $`C_{r}`$
as multimodal guidance
(Figure [4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.1 Data Construction ‣ 3 Method ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")
and
Appendix [A.3.1](#A1.SS3.SSS1 "A.3.1 Agent System Prompt ‣ A.3 Agent Prompts and Tool Schemas ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")).
A frozen video editing model $`G`$ then generates
$`\hat{V}=G(V_{s},p,C_{r})`$.

Search and reference inspection. Since training data for professional
motion editing is scarce, generative models lack the necessary prior
knowledge. To provide external knowledge to compensate for this, the
agent actively collect external references. Specifically, the agent
extracts the motion domain and specific name from the edit prompt and
calls search to obtain candidates from video platforms. The agent then
uses inspect to confirm the motion technique of the complete reference
video $`V_{r}`$ from visible demonstration, explanations, subtitles, and
on-screen text.

Clip selection and self-verification. Complete reference videos are
often noisy and too long for most video editing models to handle. To
obtain the core motion technique, the agent selects a clear, complete,
and low-interference interval from the complete reference video
$`V_{r}`$ that shows the target motion and obtains a verified reference
clip $`C_{r}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
C_{r}=\operatorname{Clip}(V_{r},[t_{s},t_{e}]),\qquad C_{r}\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{valid}}.
``` |  | (2) |

Here, $`\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{valid}}`$ denotes clips accepted by
self-verification. If $`C_{r}\notin\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{valid}}`$, the
agent re-clips $`V_{r}`$ or reselects another candidate to ensure
reference reliability.

Grounded prompt construction. The agent uses the complete reference
video $`V_{r}`$ and verified reference clip $`C_{r}`$ to obtain
sufficient professional motion knowledge. The agent then selects one of
three description formats: dense temporal, sparse stage, or key-pose.

Let $`D(V_{r},C_{r})`$ denotes the motion description, covering motion
technique, temporal structure, and motion-specific errors to avoid, and
let $`P(V_{s})`$ require all other source content to remain unchanged.
The final answer outputs a verified reference clip $`C_{r}`$ and a
grounded prompt $`p`$. The grounded prompt is

|     |                                                                |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       p=\operatorname{Compose}\bigl(u,D(V_{r},C_{r}),P(V_{s})\bigr),
       ```                                                             |     | (3) |

where $`\operatorname{Compose}`$ assembles these elements into one
natural language prompt.

### 3.3 Training Strategy

Our agent policy learns to acquire reliable, sufficient, and
generator-friendly motion guidance in two stages. We cold-start the
policy on MotionCoach-SFT-10k to establish multi-turn formatting and
basic tool use, and agentic RL on MotionCoach-RL-2k then improves the
policy through the quality of the resulting guidance and the frozen
model’s editing performance.

During the RL stage, to check whether the constructed motion guidance is
precise and sufficient, we apply a motion guidance prompt reward
$`R_{\mathrm{prompt}}`$ that compares the grounded prompt $`p`$ from the
agent policy with a teacher prompt $`p^{\star}`$,

|     |                                                               |     |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       R_{\mathrm{prompt}}=J_{\mathrm{prompt}}(V_{s},u,p^{\star},p).
       ```                                                            |     | (4) |

The function $`J_{\mathrm{prompt}}`$ scores motion correctness and
specificity, structural completeness, edit scope, and clarity, then
aggregates the scores with dimension-specific weights
(Appendix [A.3.3](#A1.SS3.SSS3 "A.3.3 Motion Guidance Prompt Reward Prompt ‣ A.3.2 Evaluation Judge Prompt ‣ A.3.1 Agent System Prompt ‣ A.3 Agent Prompts and Tool Schemas ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")).
The teacher prompt guides structure and content coverage while
equivalent wording remains acceptable.

To judge whether the constructed multimodal guidance actually supports
correct professional motion editing, we apply a motion outcome video
reward $`R_{\mathrm{video}}`$, where $`J_{\mathrm{video}}`$ scores the
outcome $`\hat{V}`$ that the frozen editing model produces from
$`V_{s}`$, $`p`$, and $`C_{r}`$ against a teacher reference $`R`$ that
represents motion knowledge,

|     |                                                           |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       R_{\mathrm{video}}=J_{\mathrm{video}}(V_{s},u,R,\hat{V}).
       ```                                                        |     | (5) |

Motion professionalism, physical plausibility, visual quality, and edit
preservation each receive a three-level score, and the weighted
aggregate emphasizes professional performance while also considering
physical plausibility and edit preservation
(Appendix [A.3.4](#A1.SS3.SSS4 "A.3.4 Motion Outcome Video Reward Judge ‣ A.3.3 Motion Guidance Prompt Reward Prompt ‣ A.3.2 Evaluation Judge Prompt ‣ A.3.1 Agent System Prompt ‣ A.3 Agent Prompts and Tool Schemas ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")).

To secure valid tool interaction and structured outputs as a basic
capability, we apply a format reward $`R_{\mathrm{format}}`$ that equals
1 when every tool call uses a valid tool name and JSON arguments and the
final answer contains a nonempty grounded prompt and one reference-clip
identifier, and 0 otherwise. The three components lie in $`[0,1]`$ and
combine as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R=\lambda_{\mathrm{prompt}}R_{\mathrm{prompt}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{video}}R_{\mathrm{video}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{format}}R_{\mathrm{format}},
``` |  | (6) |

where the format term is added separately and the weight setting follows
the ablation in
Table [9](#S4.T9 "Table 9 ‣ 4.3 Experimental Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing").
We optimize the agent policy on this reward with GRPO. Samples affected
by generation or judging infrastructure failures are excluded to avoid
attributing service errors to the agent policy.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

Training details. We train MotionCoach with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct \[[Bai
et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)\], first cold-starting the policy with SFT on
MotionCoach-SFT-10k (AdamW, learning rate $`10^{-5}`$, all parameters, 2
epochs). For RL, we run GRPO on MotionCoach-RL-2k (AdamW, learning rate
$`10^{-6}`$, task mini-batch size of 8) with 16 GPUs, plus 8 more GPUs
serving INT8 MiniMax-H3 for rollout video generation. Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B
serves as the judge for RL rewards. RL takes approximately 28 hours.
Full training details are in
Appendix [A.5](#A1.SS5 "A.5 Training and Reward Details ‣ A.4 Multi-Turn Agent Loop Example ‣ A.3.4 Motion Outcome Video Reward Judge ‣ A.3.3 Motion Guidance Prompt Reward Prompt ‣ A.3.2 Evaluation Judge Prompt ‣ A.3.1 Agent System Prompt ‣ A.3 Agent Prompts and Tool Schemas ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing").

Benchmark and evaluation. We evaluate MotionCoach on VPMEBench, which
measures professional motion editing capability, with 314 samples
covering dance, sports, and martial arts. We compare open-source
Ditto \[[Bai et al., 2026](#bib.bib8)\], Kiwi-Edit \[[Lin et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib10)\], InsV2V \[[Cheng et al., 2024](#bib.bib18)\],
Lucy-Edit-Dev \[[Team, 2025](#bib.bib11)\], MiniMax-H3 \[[MiniMax,
2026](#bib.bib12)\] and closed-source Seedance 2.0 \[[Team Seedance et
al., 2026](#bib.bib9)\], HappyHorse 1.0 \[[Alibaba Cloud,
2026](#bib.bib13)\], applying MotionCoach on the frozen MiniMax-H3 and
Seedance 2.0. Following
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Data Construction ‣ 3 Method ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing"),
we use a multimodal judge accessed through an API to score generated
videos. We report motion professionalism (MP), physical plausibility
(PP), overall video quality (VQ), and the overall score on a 100-point
scale. The overall score follows
Equation [1](#S3.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 3.1 Data Construction ‣ 3 Method ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing").
Human annotators provide pairwise judgments. QWK reaches 0.846 overall
and above 0.73 on every dimension, supporting agreement between the
automatic evaluation and human judgments
(Table [9](#S4.T9 "Table 9 ‣ 4.3 Experimental Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")
and
Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Benchmark ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")).

### 4.2 Main Results on VPMEBench

Quantitative results. As shown in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing"),
professional motion editing challenges both open-source and
closed-source video editing models: all open-source models except
MiniMax-H3 score below 50 overall, while Seedance 2.0 and HappyHorse 1.0
reach only 55.1 and 60.1 overall. Complex atomic motions often use names
rare in training data, so existing models may retain the source motion,
leading to low MP. Applying MotionCoach substantially improves the
frozen MiniMax-H3 across all reported metrics. Furthermore, when
transferred to Seedance 2.0, our method generalizes well across most
dimensions, underscoring its plug-and-play applicability. Overall, these
results show that the learned guidance-construction strategy generalizes
across video editing models.

Qualitative results. As shown in
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")(a),
existing video editing models often retain the source motion unchanged
when facing unfamiliar professional motion names. In addition, they may
misinterpret the names as unrelated visual concepts, such as generating
an actual whip object rather than the Tai Chi motion Single Whip. In
contrast, equipped with MotionCoach, video editing models successfully
generate accurate body configurations along with proper temporal
structures across dance, martial arts, and sports. Additional
qualitative results are provided in
Figure [7](#A1.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ A.2 Additional Results ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")
of
Appendix [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Additional Results ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing").

### 4.3 Experimental Analysis

Training strategy.
Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")
separates the effects of the workflow and training. The untrained
workflow yields inconsistent gains across Seedance 2.0 (SD2) and
MiniMax-H3 (H3), showing that tool access alone does not provide
reliable improvements. Subsequently, SFT consistently improves
performance across both base editors, and RL further refines the SFT
policy. The overall gains therefore stem from learning to construct
useful guidance rather than merely executing the workflow.

Multimodal input conditions.
Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")
shows that removing the grounded prompt (B) costs 13.2/15.9 points on
Seedance(SD2)/MiniMax-H3(H3), versus 5.8/0.8 for removing the reference
clip (A), since the prompt carries motion technique and temporal
structure while the clip offers complementary visual reference. Notably,
MotionCoach closely approaches expert-guided performance, trailing the
human-verified guidance (Variant D) by only 6.5/4.4 points.

Agent component.
Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")
isolates the main components. w/o Video, which replaces the reference
video with one image, reduces Overall by 10.7 and 13.2 points. w/o Clip,
which uniformly samples a five-second segment, causes drops of 8.2 and
10.4 points. w/o Verify, which removes the verify–reclip–reselect step,
causes drops of 7.5 and 9.9 points. These results show that temporal
video reference, focused clip selection, and explicit self-verification
make complementary contributions to reliable guidance construction.

Policy and tool execution.
Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")
examines where training improves the agent workflow, which reports query
accuracy (whether the target-motion name is correctly extracted),
tool-call success (whether search, inspect, and clip are executed
correctly), Pass@1 (success without retries), and trajectory success.
The largest tool-level improvement occurs in clip execution, which
increases from 62.2% to 98.3%. Training improves most stages, raising
trajectory success to 99.7%, which supports the construction of reliable
and sufficient guidance.

| Model |  | SC | BC | TF | MS | VTSS | OSC | PSC | IS | SF | CF |
| MiniMax-H3 | 48.0 | 90.9 | 95.3 | 96.5 | 98.9 | 6.4 | 19.3 | 19.1 | 2.73 | 69.5 | 1.40 |
| MiniMax-H3 + Ours | 53.8 | 92.3 | 95.2 | 97.5 | 99.0 | 6.1 | 24.5 | 19.2 | 2.62 | 95.3 | 2.05 |

Table 9: Agreement between the automatic evaluation and human judgments.

Reward weight ablation.
Table [9](#S4.T9 "Table 9 ‣ 4.3 Experimental Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")
studies the balance between the prompt and video rewards. The 0.7:0.3
ratio achieves the best Overall score of 65.61 and is used in our final
model. The prompt reward encourages precise motion specification, while
the video reward evaluates whether the resulting guidance can be
executed by the frozen editor.

Task-specific training versus model scaling. In
Table [9](#S4.T9 "Table 9 ‣ 4.3 Experimental Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing"),
all policies use the same information, tools, and inference budget.
Scaling the untrained policy from 9B to 27B improves Overall from 50.00
to 57.45 on Seedance 2.0 and from 48.87 to 56.07 on MiniMax-H3. Our
trained 8B policy reaches 65.61 and 64.46, outperforming the untrained
27B policy by 8.16 and 8.39 points. A larger backbone provides a
stronger starting point, but does not replace task-specific training.

Generalization to unseen settings. In
Table [6](#S4.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 4.3 Experimental Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing"),
we evaluate MotionCoach on the unseen subject-motion editing subset of
IVEBench. With frozen MiniMax-H3, MotionCoach raises Total from 48.0 to
53.8. Additionally, as shown in
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")(b),
we evaluate editing performance on unseen professional motion terms that
are absent from both the training data and VPMEBench, where MotionCoach
autonomously gathers domain knowledge to guide the video editing model
in executing faithful motion modifications.

\FloatBarrier

## 5 Conclusion

This work focuses on professional motion editing, which requires edited
videos to exhibit motion technique and temporal structure. We propose
MotionCoach, an agentic framework that uses multi-turn tools and
performs self-verification to get a reference clip and grounded prompt
as reliable and sufficient multimodal guidance for a frozen video
editing model. We build a trajectory data pipeline and VPMEBench, and
train the policy with agentic RL. Extensive experiments show that
MotionCoach improves professional motion editing without retraining
video editing models.

## Appendix A Appendix

### A.1 Benchmark

VPMEBench contains 314 professional motion editing tasks across 3
top-level, 10 second-level, and 25 leaf categories. Over the top-level
categories, dance holds 144 tasks (45.9%), sports and fitness holds 110
tasks (35.0%), and martial arts holds 60 tasks (19.1%).

Each task provides a human-verified five-second reference clip together
with the fine-grained annotations summarized in Figure 3(b)–(e). (b)
Temporal annotations describe each motion using one of three
structure-dependent forms: dense, sparse, or key-state, covering 191,
76, and 47 tasks, respectively. A fast Breaking move such as Noreaga
Drop receives a dense per-second timeline, a multi-stage bicycle trick
such as Back Hops is divided into a few timestamped sparse stages, and a
held yoga pose such as Warrior Two is represented by a single key state
without timestamps. (c) Reference semantic keyframes mark one to six
defining body configurations, ranging from six selected configurations
for a Tai Chi form to a single frame for a static hold, giving 1,403
keyframes across the benchmark. (d) Motion technique annotations list
the two to five execution criteria that a correct performance must
satisfy, such as pivoting the supporting foot outward during a
roundhouse kick. (e) Negative constraint annotations list the two to
four common errors to avoid, such as allowing the knee to collapse
inward.
Table [10](#A1.T10 "Table 10 ‣ A.4 Multi-Turn Agent Loop Example ‣ A.3.4 Motion Outcome Video Reward Judge ‣ A.3.3 Motion Guidance Prompt Reward Prompt ‣ A.3.2 Evaluation Judge Prompt ‣ A.3.1 Agent System Prompt ‣ A.3 Agent Prompts and Tool Schemas ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")
compares VPMEBench with representative video-editing benchmarks.
Figures [6](#A1.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ A.1 Benchmark ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")
show representative VPMEBench tasks across the dance, sports and
fitness, and martial arts top-level categories, together with the source
video, edit prompt, reference clip, semantic keyframes, and motion
annotations provided for each task.

Human validation. Before annotation, we drew a stratified random sample
of 100 paired outputs, with 50 pairs from each editor. Each pair
contained Base and Base+RL outputs generated from the same source video
and instruction, where Base denotes the frozen editor without
MotionCoach and Base+RL uses guidance from the fully trained agent. The
sample contained 46 dance, 34 sports, and 20 martial-arts pairs. We
recruited eight annotators, each with at least three years of relevant
training, coaching, performance, or competitive experience. Each pair
was independently evaluated by three annotators assigned according to
their domain expertise. Annotators had no role in method or benchmark
development. After calibration on held-out examples, they evaluated
anonymized outputs presented in randomized A/B order and selected Base
preferred, tie, or Base+RL preferred for MP, PP, VQ, and Overall. We
aggregated the three judgments for each dimension using their ordinal
median (Base preferred $`<`$ tie $`<`$ Base+RL preferred). Automatic
preferences were derived from $`\Delta`$, the Base+RL score minus the
Base score: $`|\Delta|\leq\tau`$ was treated as a tie, and the sign of
$`\Delta`$ determined the preference otherwise. We set $`\tau=3`$ points
on the 0–100 scale, based on the evaluator’s standard deviation over
five repeated judgments on a held-out calibration set. Agreement between
automatic and aggregated human preferences was measured using
quadratic-weighted kappa, reaching 0.803, 0.733, 0.943, and 0.846 for
MP, PP, VQ, and Overall, respectively. The corresponding 95% confidence
intervals are reported in
Table [9](#S4.T9 "Table 9 ‣ 4.3 Experimental Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")
and were computed using 10,000 bootstrap resamples clustered by
benchmark task.

### A.2 Additional Results

As shown in
Figure [7](#A1.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ A.2 Additional Results ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing"),
MotionCoach (blue) performs well across diverse motion-editing tasks in
dance, sports, and martial arts. Our method accurately captures
domain-specific motion patterns and key poses while preserving other
content. The first eight cases demonstrate accurate execution of the
target motions. Specifically, the six dance cases preserve their
characteristic arm and leg configurations, shoulder movements, torso
inclinations, and leg trajectories, while maintaining coordinated body
motion and smooth transitions between poses. The Taekwondo example
contains two distinct kicks with an intermediate rechambering phase,
while Kickflip captures the complete sequence of crouching, takeoff,
airborne rotation, and landing. However, the last two cases (gray)
reveal limitations in challenging settings: complex terrain can result
in an incomplete G-turn with an insufficient turning radius, while
subtle local articulations, such as the hip rotation required by the
U-shaped Hip Swing, remain difficult to perform accurately.

### A.3 Agent Prompts and Tool Schemas

We provide the agent system prompt, the prompt of the judge used for
evaluation, and the prompt of the motion guidance prompt reward judge,
together with the tool schemas, the strict per-round output format, and
the final-answer schema. We also specify the judge that produces the
motion outcome video reward during RL rollouts.

#### A.3.1 Agent System Prompt

The MotionCoach policy model receives the following system prompt in
every rollout. The same prompt is used for supervised fine-tuning, for
agentic RL rollouts, and at inference time.

`\iow_now:Ne``Ξ``\iow_now:Ne``ΞYou are an agent that constructs high-quality multimodal guidance for professional motion video editing.``\iow_now:Ne``Ξ``\iow_now:Ne``ΞYou will receive Video 1 (the source video to edit) and a short edit instruction. Call search with the extracted query˙name.``\iow_now:Ne``Ξ``\iow_now:Ne``Ξ3. Keep all non-target subjects and their actions, and all other visible content in Video 1 unchanged. Keep the action natural, continuous, and faithful to the requested mechanics and intensity. Use high-definition image quality, rich detail, cinematic quality, natural colors, and soft lighting. Keep facial features and body proportions stable and undistorted. Ensure continuous, natural motion without stiffness, interpenetration, or stuttering. Do not generate subtitles, captions, on-screen text, logos, watermarks, interface elements, or platform marks.”,”reference˙videos”:[–”video˙id”:”VID˙001”˝]˝¡/answer¿``\iow_now:Ne``Ξ``\iow_now:Ne``Ξ# Final-answer consistency rules``\iow_now:Ne``Ξ``\iow_now:Ne``Ξ- The final ¡answer¿ must contain exactly the grounded˙prompt and reference˙videos keys.``\iow_now:Ne``Ξ- grounded˙prompt must be one non-empty English grounded-prompt string, and reference˙videos must identify exactly the most recent reference clip that passed self-check.``\iow_now:Ne``Ξ- For dense mode, timestamps must be chronological and cover the useful dynamic clip without invented padding.``\iow_now:Ne``Ξ- For sparse mode, use two to four chronological timestamped phases within the self-checked clip.``\iow_now:Ne``Ξ- For single-key-state mode, use no timestamps and invent no motion sequence.``\iow_now:Ne``Ξ- Always include the exact motion name, motion-specific mechanics, positive constraints, negative constraints, and all five visible source-preservation properties.``\iow_now:Ne``Ξ- Do not output a final answer before a reference clip passes the in-trajectory self-check.`![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)` `

#### A.3.2 Evaluation Judge Prompt

The following prompt configures the multimodal judge for automatic
evaluation on VPMEBench. We adopt Gemini 3.5 Flash as the multimodal
judge. The rubric below is supplied as the system instruction. Each task
is sent as one user message containing the source video, edit
instruction, motion annotations, verified reference clip, semantic
keyframes, and generated video. The judge evaluates across multiple
dimensions, namely motion professionalism, physical plausibility, video
quality, and edit preservation, and each dimension takes only the values
0, 0.5, or 1. Decoding requests a JSON response, and a judgement is
accepted only after it validates against the schema at the end of the
rubric.

#### A.3.3 Motion Guidance Prompt Reward Prompt

Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B serves as the judge that computes the motion guidance
prompt reward $`R_{\mathrm{prompt}}`$ of
Equation [4](#S3.E4 "Equation 4 ‣ 3.3 Training Strategy ‣ 3 Method ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")
during RL rollouts. The judge receives the source video as its only
video, together with the edit instruction, the teacher grounded prompt,
and the candidate grounded prompt produced by the policy. The rubric
below is supplied as the system instruction, and the dimension
definitions are sent with every sample as a single user message in which
braces mark the fields filled per sample. The six dimensions are each
scored from 0 to 10 with weights 0.30 for instruction fidelity, 0.25 for
source-video grounding, 0.15 for motion correctness and specificity,
0.10 for template conformance, 0.15 for preservation and edit scope, and
0.05 for clarity and non-hallucination, and the weighted sum is
normalized to $`[0,1]`$. A judgement that sets hard_error caps the
reward at 0.2. Decoding uses a temperature of 0, and a judgement is
accepted only when it parses as a valid JSON object.

#### A.3.4 Motion Outcome Video Reward Judge

Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B serves as the judge that computes the motion outcome
video reward $`R_{\mathrm{video}}`$ of
Equation [5](#S3.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ 3.3 Training Strategy ‣ 3 Method ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")
during RL rollouts. Its scoring dimensions and three-level criteria are
those of the evaluation rubric in
Section [A.3.2](#A1.SS3.SSS2 "A.3.2 Evaluation Judge Prompt ‣ A.3.1 Agent System Prompt ‣ A.3 Agent Prompts and Tool Schemas ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing"),
namely motion professionalism, physical plausibility, video quality, and
edit preservation, each taking only the values 0, 0.5, or 1. Every
sample is sent as a single user message that gives the source video, a
teacher reference $`R`$ representing motion knowledge, the video
generated by the frozen video editing model, and a text part stating the
role of each video together with the short edit instruction. Decoding
uses a temperature of 0, and a judgement must be a single-line JSON
object.

### A.5 Training and Reward Details

We train the Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct policy in two stages.

#### A.5.1 Supervised Fine-Tuning

SFT uses full-parameter optimization with LLaMA-Factory and DeepSpeed
ZeRO-3.
Table [11](#A1.T11 "Table 11 ‣ A.5.1 Supervised Fine-Tuning ‣ A.5 Training and Reward Details ‣ A.4 Multi-Turn Agent Loop Example ‣ A.3.4 Motion Outcome Video Reward Judge ‣ A.3.3 Motion Guidance Prompt Reward Prompt ‣ A.3.2 Evaluation Judge Prompt ‣ A.3.1 Agent System Prompt ‣ A.3 Agent Prompts and Tool Schemas ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing")
reports the principal hyperparameters.

|----|----|
|  Base model |  Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct |
|  Training data |  MotionCoach-SFT-10k |
|  Update mode |  Full-parameter fine-tuning |
|  Hardware |  4 nodes $`\times`$ 8 GPUs |
|  Framework |  LLaMA-Factory with DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 |
|  Optimizer |  Fused AdamW ($`\beta_{1}=0.9`$, $`\beta_{2}=0.999`$, $`\epsilon=10^{-8}`$) |
|  Learning rate |  $`1\times 10^{-5}`$ |
|  Schedule |  Cosine decay; warmup ratio 0.02 |

#### A.5.2 Agentic Reinforcement Learning

In
Table [12](#A1.T12 "Table 12 ‣ A.5.2 Agentic Reinforcement Learning ‣ A.5 Training and Reward Details ‣ A.4 Multi-Turn Agent Loop Example ‣ A.3.4 Motion Outcome Video Reward Judge ‣ A.3.3 Motion Guidance Prompt Reward Prompt ‣ A.3.2 Evaluation Judge Prompt ‣ A.3.1 Agent System Prompt ‣ A.3 Agent Prompts and Tool Schemas ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing"),
RL is initialized from the final SFT checkpoint and uses full-parameter
Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) implemented on verl \[[Sheng
et al., 2025](#bib.bib33)\]. The policy-training and rollout workers
occupy two eight-GPU nodes. A third eight-GPU node serves the frozen
video editor used to generate reward videos. Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B serves as
the judge for RL rewards.
````
